text: Ponyo is a 2008 Japanese animated fantasy film written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki, animated by Studio Ghibli for the Nippon Television Network, Dentsu, Hakuhodo DY Media Partners, Buena Vista Home Entertainment, Mitsubishi, and distributed by Toho. The film stars Yuria Nara, Hiroki Doi, Tomoko Yamaguchi, Kazushige Nagashima, Yūki Amami, George Tokoro, Rumi Hiiragi, Akiko Yano, Kazuko Yoshiyuki, and Tomoko Naraoka. It is the eighth film Miyazaki directed for Studio Ghibli and his tenth overall. The story follows Ponyo, a goldfish-like creature who escapes from the ocean and is helped by a five-year-old human boy named Sōsuke after she is washed ashore while trapped in a glass jar. As they bond, Ponyo desires to become a human girl, using magic granted by Sōsuke's human blood that she licked. Fujimoto, a misanthropic wizard who was once a human, lives underwater with his daughter Brunhilde and her numerous smaller sisters, who are goldfish-like creatures with human faces. During an outing in his four-flippered submarine, Brunhilde sneaks off and floats away on a jellyfish, gets trapped in a glass jar, and is rescued by Sōsuke. When Sōsuke shatters the jar with a rock, he cuts his finger, and Brunhilde licks the blood, healing the wound instantly. Sōsuke names her Ponyo and promises to protect her. Fujimoto, distraught, searches for his daughter and calls his wave spirits to recover her, leaving Sōsuke heartbroken. Ponyo refuses to be called by her birth name, declaring her desire to be a human named Ponyo. With Sōsuke's blood, she begins transforming into a human, but Fujimoto forces her back into her true form and leaves to summon her mother, Gran Mamare. Meanwhile, Ponyo and her sisters break away and use Fujimoto's magic to become human, causing a massive release of magic that leads to a tsunami. After the tsunami, Sōsuke is overjoyed to see her, and his mother, Lisa, allows her to stay at their house. Lisa leaves to check on residents of a nursing home where she works, promising to return soon. Gran Mamare arrives at Fujimoto's submarine, where Sōsuke's father, Kōichi, recognizes her as the Goddess of Mercy. Fujimoto notices the moon falling out of orbit and satellites falling like shooting stars, signs of nature's imbalance. Gran Mamare declares that if Sōsuke passes a test, Ponyo can live as a human and nature will be restored; if he fails, Ponyo will turn into sea foam. The next day, Sōske and Ponyo find most of the land covered by the ocean. Since Lisa cannot return, they decide to find her. Using Ponyo's magic, they enlarge Sōsuke's pop-pop boat to see marine life from the Late Devonian period and more people on boats. When they reach the forest, Ponyo tires and falls asleep, and the boat reverts to its original size. Sōsuke drags Ponyo to shore, where he finds Lisa's abandoned car. As they walk, Ponyo mysteriously reverts to her fish form. Gran Mamare grants Lisa and the nursing home residents the ability to breathe underwater. Ponyo and Sōske encounter Fujimoto, who warns them about the imbalance and begs them to return Ponyo. Despite trying to escape, Fujimoto captures them and transports them to the nursing home. Sōske reunites with Lisa and meets Gran Mamare, who asks if he can love Ponyo whether she is a fish or human; Sōske confirms he does. Gran Mamare then tells Ponyo she must give up her magical powers to permanently become human. She agrees and is encased in a bubble given to Sōske, who is instructed to kiss it to complete her transformation, restoring nature's balance. The stranded ships return to port. Fujimoto respects his daughter's choice and decides to trust Sōske. Ponyo joyfully jumps and kisses Sōske, completing her transformation into a human. Miyazaki was prompted to create Ponyo after producer Toshio Suzuki suggested a film aimed at children, noting the success of Howl's Moving Castle (2004). The film combines real-world and fictional influences with new art and animation approaches developed by Studio Ghibli staff. In 2004 and 2005, Miyazaki spent time in Tomonoura, a seaside town in Setonaikai National Park, where he studied its community and environment. He read the complete works of Natsume Sōseki, particularly The Gate, which features a character named Sōsuke living at the bottom of a cliff, providing inspiration for characters and settings. Initially, Miyazaki considered a film about a stormy sea with waves higher than a house on a hillside, later creating the character Ponyo, a name he thought of as an onomatopoeia for the soft, squishy feeling of touch. He recalled borrowing Hans Christian Andersen's "The Little Mermaid" as a child and struggling with the idea that the protagonist lacked a soul. Before visiting the Tate Britain art museum, Miyazaki faced a creative block; upon seeing the 1852 painting Ophelia by John Everett Millais, he was struck by its detail and realized his animation style needed to evolve. Katsuya Kondō, who had directed the short film House Hunting (2006), was hired as animation supervisor for Ponyo and helped develop a direction emphasizing traditional hand-drawn animation with simple, solid lines. The film features frame-by-frame animation of ships, unlike typical cel animation, and the computer graphics section was closed to prioritize hand-drawn work. Elements of Richard Wagner's opera Die Walküre are present, with Ponyo's birth name, Brunhilde, referencing the Valkyrie Brünnhilde. The character of Sōsuke is based on Miyazaki's son Gorō when he was five. Miyazaki intended a sequel to Ponyo, but Toshio Suzuki convinced him to make The Wind Rises instead. The eponymous theme song, "Gake no Ue no Ponyo," was released on December 5, 2007, performed by Fujioka Fujimaki and eight-year-old Nozomi Ōhashi. It entered the Oricon Weekly Charts, reaching 6th on July 28 and 3rd on August 4, and became the 14th highest-selling single on the Oricon Yearly Charts by the end of 2008. Ōhashi was the youngest participant in the 59th NHK Kōhaku Uta Gassen at age 11, breaking Mai Hagiwara's record, and later announced the disbanding of her unit with Fujioka Fujimaki. An English-translated pop version was recorded by Jonas and Cyrus and plays over the second half of the English closing credits, with the first half being a translated version. The film score was composed by Joe Hisaishi, Miyazaki's regular collaborator, and the score album was released in Japan by Tokuma Japan Communications, in South Korea by Pony Canyon Korea, and throughout Europe by Colosseum. The film premiered in Japan on July 19, 2008, on 481 screens, a record for a domestic film, grossing ¥10 billion ($91 million) in its first month and a total of ¥15.0 billion ($153.1 million) by November 9, 2008. It was named Animation of the Year at the Tokyo Anime Fair in 2008. The film was released on VHS and DVD by Walt Disney Studios Home Entertainment on July 3, 2009, and on Blu-ray on December 8, 2009, making it the last Studio Ghibli film and the last anime film to be released on VHS, and the first Studio Ghibli film released on Blu-ray in the U.S. It was released in the U.S. and Canada on August 14, 2009, by Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures through their Walt Disney Pictures banner and The Kennedy/Marshall Company, opening in 927 theaters—the widest release for a Studio Ghibli film in the U.S., compared to Spirited Away (26), Howl's Moving Castle (36), and Princess Mononoke (38). The English dub was directed by John Lasseter, Brad Lewis, and Peter Sohn of Pixar and produced by Frank Marshall, Hayao Miyazaki, John Lasseter, Steve Alpert, and Kathleen Kennedy; the English script was written by Melissa Mathison. In July 2009, there were multiple pre-screenings in California, and Miyazaki traveled to the U.S. to promote the film at the University of California, Berkeley, and San Diego Comic-Con. The film was released in Southeast Asia on January 1, 2009. Walt Disney Studios Home Entertainment released it on DVD and Blu-ray on March 2, 2010, as the first Ghibli film directed by Miyazaki or Takahata to be released on Blu-ray in America. GKIDS re-issued it on Blu-ray and DVD on October 17, 2017, under a new deal with Studio Ghibli, and it was re-released from March 25 to 28, 2018, for its 10th anniversary. On its opening weekend in the U.S. and Canada, it earned $3,585,852 on 927 screens, with a per-screen average of $3,868, opening at number nine on the box office. The film made $15,743,471 in the U.S. and Canada and $187,461,411 in other countries for a worldwide total of $203,204,882. It received critical acclaim, with Rotten Tomatoes compiling 174 reviews and giving it a 91% positive rating with an average score of 7.6/10, and a Metacritic score of 86 out of 100 based on 29 reviews, indicating universal acclaim. The Japan Times gave it four out of five stars, praising its simple themes and visual design and comparing it to My Neighbor Totoro. Critics at the Venice International Film Festival gave high praise; Wendy Ide of The Times called it "as chaotic and exuberant as a story told by a hyperactive toddler" and gave it 4 stars out of 5, while Roger Ebert gave it four out of four stars, calling it "magical" and "visually breathtaking." The film was ranked #2 on Dentsu's list of "2008 Hit Products in Japan" after the Wii console. It was an entrant in the 65th Venice International Film Festival and received a special mention at the Bologna Future Film Festival for its high artistic and expressive quality. In 2009, it won five awards at the 8th annual Tokyo Anime Awards, including "Anime of the Year" and "Best Domestic Feature," with Miyazaki winning best director and best original story, and Noboru Yoshida winning best art direction. The film also won Animation of the Year and Outstanding Achievement in Music at the 32nd Japan Academy Prize.
